disease_info: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking and behavior, and negative symptoms such as diminished emotional expression and social withdrawal, with at least six months of disturbance and one month of active-phase symptoms. It typically emerges in late adolescence or early adulthood, but late-onset cases can occur, particularly in women and under medical or psychosocial stress. The course is often relapsing and remitting with variable functional decline, and impairment in work, relationships, or self-care is required for diagnosis. It is distinguished from mood disorders with psychotic features by the persistence of psychotic symptoms outside mood episodes and from brief or schizophreniform psychoses by its longer duration and broader impact on functioning.

narrative.stressor: About a year before presentation, Mark’s long-time regional manager retired and the chain rolled out a new inventory and scheduling system that shifted much of the forecasting responsibility onto store-level supervisors. The transition meant longer hours, tighter performance metrics, and pressure to manage abrupt schedule changes during a particularly demanding holiday season. Over the following months, his once-reliable ability to juggle complex staffing plans and inventory projections began to fall apart, leading to missed orders, chaotic shift coverage, and noticeable friction with both upper management and his associates. When his employer formally wrote him up after a series of disorganized staff meetings and customer complaints, his wife and adult son pushed for a psychiatric evaluation, recognizing that his decline in organization and judgment was far beyond normal job stress or aging.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My wife says I’ve been acting all over the place at work and at home, like I can’t control what I’m doing or keep it appropriate to what’s going on.”

narrative.stressor: Manuela’s symptoms began to emerge in the year after her husband’s death, when she went from a busy shared household to living alone for the first time in decades. Initially, her church friends and adult children attributed her increasing disorganization at potlucks and missed choir rehearsals to grief and normal aging, especially as she tried to manage bills, home repairs, and social commitments on her own. Over the next 11 months, however, her behavior at church events and the senior center grew markedly more erratic and out of step with the situation, to the point that other volunteers quietly stopped relying on her to coordinate activities. After she became unable to follow simple planning conversations and her pastor noticed that she could no longer keep her tasks straight during choir practices, her daughter accompanied her to a clinic, worried that something more serious than bereavement or forgetfulness was happening.
narrative.chief_complaint: “When I try to talk things through with people, my thoughts get all jumbled and I can’t seem to keep a straight line in a conversation anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Richard’s difficulties started after he left his community college program and took on full-time warehouse work, moving from the predictable structure of school and part-time shifts into rotating schedules and heavier responsibilities. At first his supervisors appreciated his meticulous style, but over the ensuing 11 months he became increasingly unable to maintain orderly routines, with coworkers noticing abrupt changes in how he organized pallets, followed safety procedures, and interacted during shift briefings. His family saw a stark contrast between the careful planner who once managed fishing trips and woodworking projects down to the last detail and the young man who now seemed unable to stick to basic plans or behave in ways that fit the situation at church and at home. When mounting problems at work led to a formal performance warning and his pastor mentioned being concerned about how disorganized and out of step he seemed during volunteer shifts, his parents brought him to psychiatric services for an urgent evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I can’t seem to keep my actions in order at work—I start doing things that don’t fit what I’m supposed to be doing and everything just turns into a mess.”
